[[Arlington, Texas]] | champions = [[2014 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] | heisman = [[Marcus Mariota]] ([[quarterback]], [[2014 Oregon Ducks football team|Oregon]]) | ap_poll = [[2014 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]]{{cite web|title=Final 2014 Associated Press poll has Alabama in top five as Ohio State claims title|url=http://www.al.com/alabamafootball/index.ssf/2015/01/final_2014_associated_press_po.html|website=AL.com|date=January 13, 2015 |access-date=January 14, 2015}} | coaches_poll = [[2014 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]]{{cite web|title=Final 2014 football coaches poll includes another top-5 finish for Alabama|url=http://www.al.com/alabamafootball/index.ssf/2015/01/final_2014_football_coaches_po.html|website=AL.com|date=January 13, 2015 |access-date=January 14, 2015}} }} The '''2014 NCAA Division I FBS football season''' was the highest level of [[college football]] competition in the United States organized by the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA). The regular season began on August 27, 2014, and ended on December 13, 2014. The postseason concluded on January 12, 2015, with the inaugural [[2015 College Football Playoff National Championship|College Football Playoff National Championship]] game at [[AT&T Stadium]] in [[Arlington, Texas]]. The 2014 season marked a major change to the postseason with the introduction of the [[College Football Playoff]], a four-team knockout tournament to determine the [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national champion]] of Division I FBS. The College Football Playoff system replaced the [[Bowl Championship Series]], which had been in use since [[1998 NCAA Division I-A football season|1998]]. [[2014 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State]] beat [[2014 Oregon Ducks football team|Oregon]] to claim the first ever FBS (formerly Division I-A) national title awarded using a playoff system. Following the game, Ohio State was named the No. 1 team in the [[AP Poll]] and [[Coaches' Poll]] for the season, making the Buckeyes consensus national champions among the major polls. ==Rule changes== The following rule changes have been made by the NCAA Football Rules Committee for the 2014 season:{{cite news|url=http://www.nj.com/rutgersfootball/index.ssf/2014/02/proposed_ncaa_rule_to_slow_hurry-up_offenses_draws_criticism_from_coaches.html |title=Proposed NCAA rule change to slow "hurry up offenses" draws criticism from coaches|author=NJ.com |work=nj.com |date=February 13, 2014 |access-date=February 13, 2014}} * Modifying the "targeting" rule enacted for the [[2013 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2013 season]] whereby if a targeting ejection is overturned on review, the 15 yard penalty will be overturned as well, unless the foul was committed in conjunction with another foul (such as an above-the-shoulders hit on a quarterback not deemed as targeting, a [[roughing the passer]] penalty would still apply). *Targeting definition expanded from "Initiate contact" to "Make forcible contact" and defining that any forcible contact with the crown of the helmet to an opponent is a targeting foul. * Allowing all conferences the option to experiment with eight-man officiating crews. The [[Big 12 Conference]] experimented with eight-man officiating crews during the [[2013 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2013 season]]. The eighth official is referred to as the "Center Judge", positioned opposite the Referee in the offensive backfield, and wears a "C" on the shirt. In 2014, the [[Atlantic Coast Conference]], [[Big Ten Conference]], [[Big 12 Conference]], the [[Mountain West Conference]], and the [[American Athletic Conference]] used eight-official crews. The [[Southeastern Conference]] experimented with eight officials in selected games in the 2014 season. The [[Pac-12 Conference]] made no plans to implement eight-official crews. The eight-man crews were used in bowl games (including the [[2015 College Football Playoff National Championship]]) if one of the conferences (Big 12, Big Ten, ACC, MW, or American) provided a crew for a particular game.{{cite news|url=http://newsok.com/big-12-officiating-eight-man-crews-are-here-to-stay/article/5005148 |title=Big 12 Officiating Eight-Man Crews are here to stay|work=NewsOK.com |date=July 17, 2014 |access-date=August 4, 2014}} * Modifying the 15-yard [[roughing the passer]] penalty to include hits (including lunging and/or rolling) at or below the knees from defenders that are not fouled/blocked into the quarterback, not engaged in tackling the quarterback, or are rushing unabated to the quarterback (similar to the [[National Football League|NFL's]] "[[Tom Brady]]" Rule adopted in the [[2009 NFL season]]). *The [[chain crew]] will work the first half on the same side as the press box, then switch to the side opposite the press box for the second half, the procedure used in the NFL. Prior to 2014, the chain crew worked the entire game on the sideline opposite the press box, the procedure used in high school football. A rule meant to slow down the [[hurry-up offense]] by preventing teams from snapping the ball within the first ten seconds of the 40-second play clock to allow for defensive substitutions, or be penalized five yards for [[delay of game]] (except within the final 2:00 of each half or when the play clock is set to 25 seconds) was tabled by the Rules Committee and not voted on.{{cite news|url=http://www.cbssports.com/collegefootball/eye-on-college-football/24469570/report-rules-committee-will-not-vote-on-10-second-rule |title=Report: Rules Committee Will Not Vote On "10 Second Rule"|author=CBSSports.com |work=CBSSports.com |date=March 5, 2014 |access-date=March 5, 2014}} ==Conference realignment== {{Main|2010–2014 NCAA conference realignment}} {{see also|2010–14 Big Ten Conference realignment}} ===Membership changes=== [[Appalachian State Mountaineers football|Appalachian State]], [[Georgia Southern Eagles football|Georgia Southern]] and [[Old Dominion Monarchs football|Old Dominion]] moved from the [[Football Championship Subdivision]] (FCS) to FBS. 2014 was expected to be the final season for [[UAB Blazers football|UAB football]], who dropped their program at the conclusion of the season due to financial reasons. Athletic Conference|The American]]}} |- | [[Western Kentucky Hilltoppers football|Western Kentucky]] | [[Sun Belt Conference|Sun Belt]] |[[Conference USA]] |- |} ==Other headlines== * May 14 ** The NCAA announced its [[Academic Progress Rate]] (APR) sanctions for the 2014–15 school year. Two FBS teams, [[2014 Idaho Vandals football team|Idaho]] and [[2014 UNLV Rebels football team|UNLV]], were among the 36 programs in 11 sports declared ineligible for postseason play due to failure to meet the required APR benchmark.{{cite press release|url=https://www.ncaa.org/about/resources/media-center/news/student-athletes-continue-achieve-academically |title=Student-Athleties Continue To Achieve Academically |publisher=NCAA |date=May 14, 2014 |access-date=May 14, 2014}} ** [[Boise State Broncos football|Boise State]] announced that it had received a waiver from the NCAA allowing the school to immediately provide assistance to incoming freshman recruit Antoine Turner, a defensive end originally from [[New Orleans]] who had been [[Homelessness in the United States|homeless]] due to financial and family issues.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/10931580/boise-state-broncos-allowed-ncaa-provide-immediate-assistance-incoming-recruit-antoine-turner |title=Boise State can help Antoine Turner |first=Joe |last=Schad |work=ESPN.com |date=May 14, 2014 |access-date=May 14, 2014}} * June 26 – UNLV announced that the school would be eligible for postseason after the upcoming season; they stated that the NCAA had accepted an updated Academic Progress Rate score submitted by the university.{{cite news|url=http://www.lasvegassun.com/news/2014/jun/26/unlv-footballs-bowl-ban-lifted/|title=UNLV football's postseason ban is lifted this season|newspaper=[[Las Vegas Sun]] |date=June 26, 2014 |access-date=June 28, 2014}} *September 8 – The NCAA restored [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State's]] postseason eligibility effective immediately, and full complement of 85 scholarships effective with the 2015 season. This means Penn State could qualify for a bowl game for the 2014 season. Penn State was originally banned from postseason play from 2012 to 2015 because of [[Penn State child sex abuse scandal|the Jerry Sandusky child abuse scandal]].{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11489258/ncaa-drops-postseason-ban-penn-state-nittany-lions |title=Penn State's postseason ban over |first=Josh |last=Moyer |work=ESPN.com |date=September 8, 2014 |access-date=September 8, 2014}} * October 4 ** For the first time since Week 11 of the [[1990 NCAA Division I-A football season|1990 season]],{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11647045/mississippi-rebels-mississippi-state-bulldogs-tied-third-associated-press-college-football-poll|title=Florida State, Auburn 1-2 in AP poll|date=October 5, 2014|access-date=October 5, 2014|work=ESPN.com}} four teams ranked in the top six of the [[AP Poll]] lost during the week. Additionally, five of the top eight of the AP Poll lost in the same week for the first time ever.{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/page/gamedayfinal100414/chaos-wins-week-6-college-football-playoff-contenders-were-upset |title=The winner in Week 6? Chaos |first1=Chris |last1=Low |first2=Mark |last2=Schlabach |work=ESPN.com |date=October 5, 2014 |access-date=October 5, 2014}} The week's upsets began on Thursday, when No. 2 [[2014 Oregon Ducks football team|Oregon]] lost 31–24 at home to [[2014 Arizona Wildcats football team|Arizona]]. Saturday saw No. 3 [[2014 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]] lose 23–17 at No. 11 [[2014 Ole Miss Rebels football team|Ole Miss]], No. 4 [[2014 Oklahoma Sooners football team|Oklahoma]] lose 37–33 at No. 25 [[2014 TCU Horned Frogs football team|TCU]], No. 6 [[2014 Texas A&M Aggies football team|Texas A&M]] lose 48–31 at No. 12 [[2014 Mississippi State Bulldogs football team|Mississippi State]], and No. 8 [[2014 UCLA Bruins football team|UCLA]] lose 30–28 at home to [[2014 Utah Utes football team|Utah]]. ** [[2014 Washington State Cougars football team|Washington State]] quarterback [[Connor Halliday]] set a new FBS record for single-game passing yards, throwing for 734 yards in a 60–59 loss to [[2014 California Golden Bears football team|Cal]]. This broke the previous record of 716, set in 1990 by [[Houston Cougars football|Houston's]] [[David Klingler]], and was five short of the all-divisions NCAA record of 739 set by Sam Durley of [[NCAA Division III|Division III]] [[Eureka College|Eureka]] in 2012. In the same game, Cal's [[Jared Goff]] threw for 527 yards, giving the two teams an FBS-record 1,261 passing yards in the game.{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11645936/washington-state-cougars-qb-connor-halliday-sets-fbs-single-game-passing-record-734-yards-california-golden-bears |title=Connor Halliday sets passing record |first=Kyle |last=Bonagura |work=ESPN.com |date=October 5, 2014 |access-date=October 5, 2014}} * October 12 – The release of the Week 8 AP Poll saw Mississippi State, previously tied for No. 3 with [[Egg Bowl|cross-state rival]] Ole Miss, leapfrog [[2014 Florida State Seminoles football team|Florida State]] to reach No. 1 for the first time in school history. Mississippi State had just beaten No. 2 [[2014 Auburn Tigers football team|Auburn]] at home by a score of 38–23, the Bulldogs' third straight over a team then ranked in the top 10. Most significantly, the Bulldogs became the first team in the history of the AP Poll to go from unranked to No. 1 in five weeks, surpassing the previous record of six weeks set by [[1954 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State in 1954]].{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11688921/mississippi-state-bulldogs-rise-no-1-associated-press-college-football-poll |title=Mississippi State No. 1 in AP poll |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=October 12, 2014 |access-date=October 13, 2014}} * October 18 – [[2014 Marshall Thundering Herd football team|Marshall]] quarterback [[Rakeem Cato]] threw for four touchdowns in the Thundering Herd's 45–13 win at [[2014 FIU Panthers football team|FIU]], giving him a touchdown pass in 39 consecutive games. This broke a tie for the FBS record with [[Russell Wilson]], who threw for TDs in 38 consecutive games while at [[NC State Wolfpack football|NC State]] and [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin]].{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400548050 |title=Cato gets record; No. 25 Marshall tops FIU 45-13 |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=October 18, 2014 |access-date=October 18, 2014}} Cato went on to finish the season and his Marshall career in the [[2014 Boca Raton Bowl|Boca Raton Bowl]] with a streak of 46 games, tying the all-divisions NCAA record of [[Central Washington Wildcats|Central Washington's]] [[Mike Reilly (quarterback)|Mike Reilly]].{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400610203 |title=Rakeem Cato ties TD mark as Marshall wins Boca Raton Bowl |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=December 23, 2014 |access-date=December 24, 2014}} * November 16 – [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin]] running back [[Melvin Gordon]] set a new FBS record with 408 rushing yards in the [[2014 Wisconsin Badgers football team|Badgers]]' 59–24 win over [[2014 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|Nebraska]]. The previous record of 406 yards had been set by [[TCU Horned Frogs football|TCU's]] [[LaDainian Tomlinson]] in 1999.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap/_/gameId/400547974 |title=Melvin Gordon sets FBS rushing record with 408 yards vs. Huskers |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=November 16, 2014 |access-date=December 2, 2014}} * November 22 – Melvin Gordon's single-game FBS rushing record, which had been set less than a week earlier, is broken by [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma's]] [[Samaje Perine]], who ran for 427 yards in the [[2014 Oklahoma Sooners football team|Sooners]]' 44–7 win over [[2014 Kansas Jayhawks football team|Kansas]].{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap/_/gameId/400547894 |title= Samaje Perine runs for FBS-record 427 yards as Oklahoma routs Kansas |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=November 16, 2014 |access-date=December 2, 2014}} * November 29 – [[2014 Louisville Cardinals football team|Louisville]] safety [[Gerod Holliman]] intercepted his 14th pass of the season, tying the single-season FBS record set in 1968 by [[Washington Huskies football|Washington's]] [[Al Worley]]. The interception in the final minute sealed the Cardinals' 44–40 win over [[Governor's Cup (Kentucky)|archrival]] [[2014 Kentucky Wildcats football team|Kentucky]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/louisville-s-gerod-holliman-ties-single-season-interception-mar-0ap3000000435886 |title=Louisville's Gerod Holliman ties single-season interception mark |first=Mike |last=Huguenin |work=[[NFL.com]] |date=November 29, 2014 |access-date=December 11, 2014}} * November 30 – Police in [[Columbus, Ohio]] discovered the body of [[Kosta Karageorge]], a [[Ohio State Buckeyes wrestling|wrestler]] at [[Ohio State University|Ohio State]] who had walked on to the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|football team]] but had yet to appear in a game. Karageorge, who disappeared on November 26, was found with an apparently self-inflicted gunshot wound. He had been complaining about post-concussion symptoms in the last weeks of his life.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11960455/kosta-karageorge-ohio-state-buckeyes-found-dead |title=Body identified as Kosta Karageorge |first=Austin |last=Ward |work=ESPN.com |date=December 1, 2014 |access-date=December 2, 2014}} * December 2 – [[UAB Blazers football|UAB]] announced that it would drop football at the end of [[2014 UAB Blazers football team|the season]]. The Blazers, under first-year head coach [[Bill Clark (American football)|Bill Clark]], became bowl-eligible for only the second time in program history with a win on November 29 over [[2014 Southern Miss Golden Eagles football team|Southern Miss]]. UAB became the first FBS-level program to fold since [[Pacific Tigers football|Pacific]] dropped football after the 1995 season.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/11967626/uab-blazers-shut-football-program |title=UAB shutting down football program |work=ESPN.com |date=December 2, 2014 |access-date=December 2, 2014}} (The Blazers would ultimately reinstate football in [[2017 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2017]].) * December 5 – The board of governors of [[Colorado State University|Colorado State]] approved the construction of a new on-campus stadium to replace the [[Colorado State Rams football|Rams]]' then-current off-campus home of [[Sonny Lubick Field at Hughes Stadium|Hughes Stadium]]. No date for completion had been set; potential capacities ranged from 35,872 to 41,200.{{cite news |url=http://collegefootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/12/05/board-of-regents-approve-new-on-campus-stadium-for-colorado-state-rams/related/ |title=Board of Governors approve new on-campus stadium for Colorado State Rams |first=Brent |last=Sobleski |work=College Football Talk |publisher=NBCSports.com |date=December 5, 2014 |access-date=December 6, 2014 |archive-date=December 8, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141208133731/http://collegefootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/12/05/board-of-regents-approve-new-on-campus-stadium-for-colorado-state-rams/related/ |url-status=dead }} The venue would open in 2017 as Colorado State Stadium with the full 41,200 capacity, and since 2018 has been known as [[Canvas Stadium]]. * December 8 – ''[[Sporting News]]'' reported that the Big 12 Conference had been planning to expand beyond its current ten teams even before being left out of the inaugural College Football Playoff. Specifically, conference officials met with officials from the [[University of Cincinnati]].{{cite magazine|url=http://www.sportingnews.com/ncaa-basketball/story/2014-12-08/college-football-playoff-big-12-expansion-champions-bob-bowlsby-cincinnati-memphis-byu |title=Big 12 researching possible candidates for expansion even before playoff snub |first=Mike |last=DeCourcy |magazine=Sporting News |date=December 8, 2014 |access-date=December 9, 2014}} These expansion plans were later dropped. ==Updated stadiums== === New stadiums === *'''[[Baylor Bears football|Baylor]]''' opened '''[[McLane Stadium]]''', returning home games to its campus for the first time since 1935. The stadium opened with 42,000 permanent seats plus 3,000 standing-room places, and is designed for future expansion to 55,000. The first game was a [[High school football|high school]] contest on August 29;{{cite news|title=Aledo Will Play Cedar Park in First Game at Baylor's New McLane Stadium |first=Matt |last=Wixon |url=http://highschoolsportsblog.dallasnews.com/2014/03/aledo-will-play-cedar-park-in-first-game-at-baylors-new-mclane-stadium.html/ |newspaper=[[The Dallas Morning News]] |date=March 5, 2014 |access-date=August 30, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140327234518/http://highschoolsportsblog.dallasnews.com/2014/03/aledo-will-play-cedar-park-in-first-game-at-baylors-new-mclane-stadium.html/ |archive-date=March 27, 2014 }} Baylor's first game was a 45–0 win over [[2014 SMU Mustangs football team|SMU]] on August 31.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400547648 |title=No. 10 Baylor opens stadium with 45-0 win over SMU |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=September 1, 2014}} *'''[[Houston Cougars football|Houston]]''' opened '''[[TDECU Stadium]]''', a 40,000-seat venue, designed to be easily expandable to 60,000, and built on the site of the school's former [[Robertson Stadium]]. The opening game was a 27–7 loss to [[2014 UTSA Roadrunners football team|UTSA]] on August 29.{{cite news|url=http://blog.chron.com/sportsupdate/2014/08/gameday-central-uh-opens-tdecu-stadium-against-utsa/ |title=Cougars suffer ugly 27-7 loss to UTSA in TDECU Stadium's first game |first=Jonathan |last=Feigen |newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]] |date=August 29, 2014 |access-date=August 30, 2014}} *'''[[Tulane Green Wave football|Tulane]]''' opened '''[[Yulman Stadium]]''', a 30,000-seat on-campus venue located near the former site of [[Tulane Stadium]]. This returned home games to the Tulane campus for the first time since 1974, the year before the [[Mercedes-Benz Superdome|Superdome]] opened. The first game was a 38–21 loss to [[2014 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team|Georgia Tech]] on September 6.{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400547656 |title= Zenon, Byerly power G. Tech past Tulane 38-21 |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |date=September 6, 2014 |access-date=September 6, 2014}} The three schools that moved from FCS to FBS this season use existing on-campus stadiums: *'''[[Appalachian State Mountaineers football|Appalachian State]]''' plays at '''[[Kidd Brewer Stadium]]''', home to the Mountaineers since 1962 and affectionately known to the school's fans as "The Rock". It has an official capacity of 24,050, but has frequently hosted significantly larger crowds, with the record being 31,531. *'''[[Georgia Southern Eagles football|Georgia Southern]]''' plays at '''[[Paulson Stadium]]''', home to the Eagles since 1984. The stadium was expanded to 24,300 for GSU's move to FBS. *'''[[Old Dominion Monarchs football|Old Dominion]]''' plays at '''[[Foreman Field]]'''. The 20,118-seat stadium first opened in 1936 for the football program of what was then known as the Norfolk Division of The College of William & Mary. After football was dropped after the 1941 season, the stadium was used for other football games (notably the former [[Oyster Bowl]]), plus other ODU sports, until the school reinstated football in [[2009 Old Dominion Monarchs football team|2009]]. === Renovated stadiums === *'''[[LSU Tigers football|LSU]]''' opened a new south end-zone upper deck expansion of [[Tiger Stadium (LSU)|Tiger Stadium]] that added approximately 60 "Tiger Den" suites, 3,000 club seats and 1,500 general public seats and brought the total capacity to approximately 102,321, making it the seventh-largest college football stadium in the country. *'''[[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State]]''' added 2,500 seats to the south stands of [[Ohio Stadium]]. These seats, built over the entrance tunnels, raised the official capacity of the stadium to 104,851, making it the third-largest stadium in the country and the fifth-largest stadium in the world. *'''[[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M]]''' opened Phase 1 of a major three-year renovation of [[Kyle Field]], which includes re-construction of the east side first deck, and construction of the south end zone, which in turn includes seating, media interview areas, 12th Man Productions and related gameday support, a commissary and recruiting area. *'''[[Mississippi State Bulldogs football|Mississippi State]]''' opened a new north end-zone expansion of [[Davis Wade Stadium]] which took stadium capacity from 55,000 to over 61,000. The renovation created new concessions and restrooms, plus a new west side concourse. *'''[[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri]]''' opened a new east side expansion of [[Faurot Field]]. An upper bowl was completed for the east side of the stadium, providing 5,200 general admission seats and 800 club seats. *'''[[Louisiana Ragin' Cajuns football|Louisiana-Lafayette]]''' enclosed the south side of [[Cajun Field]]. The stadium upgrade added 5,900 seats increasing the capacity from 31,000 to 36,900. *'''[[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue]]''' removed the majority of their south end-zone bleachers at [[Ross–Ade Stadium]] and replaced it with a patio area. This stadium upgrade lowered the stadium capacity from 62,500 to 57,236. * The '''[[Rose Bowl (stadium)|Rose Bowl]]''' opened the final phase of its multi-year renovation project, which included the removal of seats on the east and west sidelines to restore the original oval shape of the seating bowl. Also included in the project were additional new restrooms, new entry gate structures, and additional new concession stands. The historic hedges surrounding the field were restored to create a new "Rose Garden Walkway". An iconic plaza opened outside of Gate A in front of the south main entrance to the stadium, featuring a large logo of the [[Pasadena Tournament of Roses]]. === Other === * [[Eastern Michigan Eagles football|'''Eastern Michigan''']] installed a gray [[FieldTurf]] playing surface at '''[[Rynearson Stadium]]'''. The stadium is only the second FBS venue with a [[List of college football venues with non-traditional field colors|non-traditional field color]], after [[Albertsons Stadium]] at [[Boise State Broncos football|Boise State]], and the sixth college stadium overall with this feature.{{cite press release |url=http://www.emueagles.com/news/2014/6/17/FB_0617141758.aspx?path=football |title=EMU Installing Gray FieldTurf Surface at Rynearson Stadium |publisher=[[Eastern Michigan Eagles|Eastern Michigan University Athletics]] |date=June 17, 2014 |access-date=June 23, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190326144536/https://emueagles.com/news/2014/6/17/FB_0617141758.aspx?path=football |archive-date=March 26, 2019 |url-status=dead }} ==Regular season top 10 matchups== Rankings reflect the [[AP Poll]].
